PHASE 7 · FNP CERTIFICATION REVIEW & CLINICAL INTEGRATION

Week 156 — Lesson 180: Older Adult & Geriatric Clinical Integration Board Review

FNP-level goal: Integrate acute illness, cognition, function, mobility, medications, multimorbidity, sensory status, caregiver capacity, social vulnerability, prognosis, and what matters most to recognize reversible threats and create safe, individualized care for older adults.

Learning Objectives

  • Use the Geriatrics 5Ms to organize complex primary-care and board-style cases.
  • Distinguish delirium, dementia, depression, medication effects, and other causes of cognitive or functional change.
  • Assess falls, frailty, orthostasis, mobility, ADLs, IADLs, nutrition, continence, sensory loss, and caregiver strain.
  • Perform medication reconciliation and deprescribing reasoning without treating age or a screening list as an automatic stop order.
  • Recognize atypical presentations of infection, cardiovascular disease, metabolic illness, trauma, and medication toxicity.
  • Apply decision-specific capacity assessment, supported decision-making, advance care planning, and goal-concordant treatment.
  • Identify elder mistreatment, unsafe living conditions, driving risk, and transitions that require urgent intervention.
  • Close care gaps through interprofessional planning, explicit follow-up ownership, and reassessment after every transition or medication change.

Part 1 — The Geriatrics 5Ms

Chronologic age alone does not define an older adult’s health, prognosis, or treatment goals. Two people of the same age may differ profoundly in reserve, cognition, function, social support, treatment burden, and priorities. The Geriatrics 5Ms organize this complexity:

  • Mind: cognition, delirium, dementia, depression, sleep, and emotional health.
  • Mobility: gait, balance, falls, transfers, strength, pain, and access to assistive devices.
  • Medications: indication, effectiveness, interactions, adverse effects, adherence, affordability, and deprescribing.
  • Multicomplexity: multiple conditions, frailty, social vulnerability, caregiver capacity, prognosis, and competing recommendations.
  • Matters Most: the patient’s goals, acceptable tradeoffs, preferred function, living situation, and care priorities.

The 5Ms are not five independent checkboxes. A sedating medication may worsen Mind and Mobility; a fall may change what Matters Most; financial barriers may make a theoretically ideal regimen unsafe.

Part 2 — Function Is a Vital Sign

Disease labels and laboratory values do not reveal whether a patient can bathe, dress, transfer, prepare food, manage medication, use a phone, pay bills, or obtain transportation. Functional change may be the earliest sign of illness and often predicts real-world risk more directly than a single biomarker.

Ask what the patient could do before the current problem, what changed, when it changed, and what help is now required. Compare baseline with today. A new inability to walk to the bathroom after a “minor” infection represents meaningful deterioration even if the temperature and white count are normal.

Part 3 — ADLs and IADLs

Activities of daily living (ADLs) include basic self-care such as bathing, dressing, toileting, transferring, continence, and feeding. Instrumental activities of daily living (IADLs) require more complex executive function, including shopping, cooking, transportation, medication management, finances, housekeeping, and communication.

IADL decline may precede ADL loss in cognitive disease. Determine whether assistance is new, who provides it, whether that support is reliable, and whether the patient is safe when alone. Function should be reassessed after hospitalization, delirium, falls, medication changes, and major illness.

Part 4 — Frailty Is Reduced Physiologic Reserve

Frailty describes vulnerability to disproportionate decline after a stressor. A urinary infection, new medication, or brief hospitalization may cause delirium, falls, immobility, and loss of independence in a frail person while a more robust adult recovers quickly.

Clues include slowed gait, weakness, exhaustion, weight loss, low activity, recurrent falls, prolonged recovery, and increasing dependence. Frailty is not identical to age, disability, or comorbidity. Recognizing it should prompt risk reduction, realistic treatment planning, nutrition and exercise support, medication review, and discussion of patient priorities—not therapeutic abandonment.

Part 5 — Homeostasis Changes With Aging

Older adults often have less renal reserve, altered body composition, impaired thirst, reduced baroreflex response, slower drug clearance, and diminished ability to respond to heat, cold, dehydration, infection, and acute stress. Illness may therefore appear as weakness, confusion, a fall, anorexia, or functional decline rather than a classic symptom.

Do not call a dangerous presentation “just aging.” Aging changes presentation and reserve; it does not explain an acute deviation from baseline.

Part 6 — Atypical Presentation Is Still Real Disease

Myocardial ischemia may present with dyspnea, fatigue, nausea, syncope, or confusion rather than chest pain. Infection may occur without high fever or leukocytosis. Hyperthyroidism may appear as weight loss and atrial fibrillation rather than tremor and heat intolerance. Medication toxicity may look like a new neurologic disorder.

Board questions often signal serious disease through a change in function, appetite, cognition, or falls. Build a problem representation around tempo, baseline, physiology, and medications rather than waiting for textbook symptoms.

Part 7 — Delirium: Acute Brain Failure

Delirium is an acute, fluctuating disturbance of attention and awareness with an underlying medical, toxic, environmental, or withdrawal cause. It can be hyperactive, hypoactive, or mixed. Hypoactive delirium is easily missed because the patient may simply appear quiet, sleepy, or disengaged.

Core clues are hours-to-days onset, fluctuation, impaired attention, and altered level of awareness. Dementia is usually chronic and progressive, but dementia strongly increases delirium risk. When uncertain, treat an acute change as delirium until reversible threats are assessed.

Part 8 — Delirium Differential

Common contributors include infection, hypoxia, hypoglycemia, stroke, seizure, pain, urinary retention, constipation, dehydration, organ failure, electrolyte or endocrine disturbance, medication toxicity, anticholinergic burden, sedatives, alcohol or benzodiazepine withdrawal, sleep disruption, and an unfamiliar environment.

More than one cause is common. A positive urinalysis does not close the case: the patient may also have dehydration, medication accumulation, hypoxia, or intracranial injury. Test according to history, examination, risk, and physiology rather than ordering an indiscriminate panel.

Part 9 — Delirium Is an Emergency Signal

Check airway, breathing, circulation, oxygenation, glucose, vital signs, neurologic deficits, trauma, and toxic exposure first. Determine last known baseline and obtain collateral history from someone who knows the patient. Review every prescription, over-the-counter product, supplement, recent dose change, and access to another person’s medication.

New focal deficit, severe headache, seizure, head trauma, hypoxia, hemodynamic instability, meningismus, severe agitation that threatens safety, or inability to maintain hydration requires emergency evaluation. Avoid reflexively sedating a patient before searching for pain, retention, hypoxia, or another reversible driver.

Part 10 — Dementia Is Not Normal Aging

Dementia describes acquired cognitive decline that interferes with independence. Domains may include memory, executive function, language, visuospatial ability, social cognition, and complex attention. Establish the trajectory, affected activities, safety consequences, neurologic findings, mood, sleep, substance exposure, and medication burden.

Screening tools identify concern; they do not determine etiology or capacity. Evaluate potentially reversible or contributing conditions when clinically indicated, and distinguish neurodegenerative disease from depression, delirium, sensory impairment, medication effects, sleep apnea, metabolic disease, and structural neurologic pathology.

Part 11 — Delirium vs Dementia vs Depression

  • Delirium: acute or subacute, fluctuating, impaired attention, altered awareness; urgent search for a cause.
  • Dementia: chronic progressive decline that disrupts independence; attention may be relatively preserved early.
  • Depression: mood, anhedonia, sleep, energy, guilt, concentration, appetite, psychomotor, and suicide symptoms; cognitive complaints may coexist.

These conditions can occur together. A person with dementia can develop delirium and depression. Choose the next action from the current safety threat and tempo, not from a false either-or distinction.

Part 12 — Capacity Is Decision-Specific

Decision-making capacity is a clinical determination about a particular choice at a particular time. Assess whether the patient can communicate a choice, understand relevant information, appreciate how it applies personally, and reason about options and consequences.

A dementia diagnosis does not automatically remove capacity, and an unwise choice does not by itself prove incapacity. Optimize hearing, vision, language access, pain, medication effects, and delirium before assessment. Capacity can fluctuate and the threshold for certainty rises with the risk and complexity of the decision. Legal competency is determined through a legal process, not casually declared in clinic.

Part 13 — Supported Decision-Making

Use plain language, small information segments, teach-back, hearing or visual aids, interpreters, and trusted supporters chosen by the patient. Preserve autonomy to the greatest extent possible. If capacity is absent, identify the legally authorized surrogate and use known preferences, advance directives, and substituted judgment or best-interest standards as applicable.

Family presence can help but should not erase the patient’s voice. Interview the patient directly and privately when needed, especially if coercion, exploitation, or mistreatment is possible.

Part 14 — Falls Are a Syndrome, Not a Diagnosis

Ask about falls in the past year, near-falls, injury, circumstances, prodrome, loss of consciousness, footwear, assistive device, environmental hazards, and ability to rise. A “mechanical fall” may still result from orthostasis, arrhythmia, neuropathy, sedatives, poor vision, muscle weakness, hypoglycemia, infection, stroke, or unsafe surroundings.

After a fall, first assess injury and immediate cause. Head impact, anticoagulant or antiplatelet exposure, focal deficit, persistent vomiting, severe pain, inability to bear weight, syncope, or hemodynamic abnormality raises urgency.

Part 15 — STEADI: Screen, Assess, Intervene

CDC’s STEADI framework uses three practical steps: screen for fall risk, assess modifiable risk factors, and intervene. Assessment may include gait and balance, orthostatic blood pressure, medication review, vision, feet and footwear, home hazards, cognition, strength, continence urgency, cardiovascular symptoms, and vitamin or bone-health issues when clinically relevant.

USPSTF recommends exercise interventions for community-dwelling adults 65 or older who are at increased fall risk and individualized decisions about multifactorial interventions. Exercise should match ability and can address balance, strength, and gait. A brochure alone is not a fall-prevention program.

Part 16 — Orthostatic Symptoms Need a Mechanism

Clarify dizziness, weakness, visual dimming, falls, meals, heat, hydration, timing, and medication relationship. Measure blood pressure and pulse with an appropriate supine-to-standing protocol when safe. Consider volume depletion, blood loss, autonomic dysfunction, deconditioning, venous pooling, and medications such as antihypertensives, diuretics, vasodilators, and psychoactive drugs.

Treatment targets the cause and the patient’s priorities. Do not simply discontinue every blood-pressure medication or accept recurrent syncope. Chest symptoms, exertional events, arrhythmia concern, injury, severe anemia, or persistent hypotension may require urgent evaluation.

Part 17 — Syncope Is Not the Same as a Fall

Determine whether there was transient loss of consciousness, sudden loss of postural tone, prodrome, seizure activity, exertion, palpitations, injury, or post-event confusion. Collateral history is often decisive. High-risk features include exertional syncope, abnormal ECG, structural heart disease, family history of sudden death, severe anemia or bleeding, persistent neurologic findings, or unstable vital signs.

Labeling an unwitnessed event as a trip can delay recognition of arrhythmia, orthostasis, hemorrhage, or seizure.

Part 18 — Mobility Includes More Than Walking

Assess rising from a chair, transfers, turning, gait speed, balance, endurance, pain, fear of falling, and correct use of cane or walker. Functional mobility depends on vision, vestibular function, sensation, strength, joints, cognition, environment, and confidence.

Bed rest accelerates deconditioning. After illness or hospitalization, ask whether the patient returned to baseline and arrange physical or occupational therapy, home safety evaluation, pain management, and equipment when indicated. Mobility plans should support what matters most, not merely reduce a test score.

Part 19 — Polypharmacy Means Risk, Not a Number Alone

Medication harm arises from drug-drug and drug-disease interactions, prescribing cascades, duplicate therapy, confusing schedules, renal or hepatic impairment, affordability, and failure to stop drugs after the original indication ends. A complete list includes prescriptions, PRN medications, over-the-counter products, sleep aids, anticholinergics, supplements, alcohol, and medications from multiple prescribers.

For every drug, ask: What is the indication? Is it helping? What harm is possible now? Is the dose appropriate for current kidney and liver function? Does it align with goals and prognosis? Who monitors it, and when can it be reduced or stopped?

Part 20 — Beers Criteria Are a Conversation Starter

The AGS Beers Criteria identify potentially inappropriate medications, important drug-disease interactions, drugs to use with caution, combinations to avoid, and medications requiring renal adjustment. They support review but do not replace clinical judgment or patient preference.

A listed medication is not automatically forbidden, and an unlisted medication is not automatically safe. Consider indication, alternatives, prior response, withdrawal risk, treatment duration, goals, and monitoring. Never abruptly stop a medication that requires tapering simply because it appears on a list.

Part 21 — High-Risk Medication Patterns

Watch for cumulative anticholinergic burden, sedative combinations, opioids with benzodiazepines or other respiratory depressants, hypoglycemia-producing regimens, anticoagulants without clear monitoring, NSAIDs in kidney disease or heart failure, and medications that worsen orthostasis, urinary retention, constipation, cognition, or falls.

A prescribing cascade occurs when an adverse effect is mistaken for a new disease and another drug is added. Examples include treating medication-related edema, tremor, constipation, or confusion without reconsidering the original drug.

Part 22 — Deprescribing Is Active Care

Prioritize drugs with no current indication, high harm, duplication, low time-to-benefit relative to prognosis, or poor alignment with goals. Agree on what to stop first, whether tapering is required, which symptoms to monitor, and when to follow up. Change a manageable number of medications at once so effects can be understood.

Deprescribing is not denial of treatment. It is supervised reduction of treatment burden and avoidable harm while preserving therapies that improve symptoms, function, or meaningful outcomes.

Part 23 — Kidney Function and Medication Accumulation

Serum creatinine may appear deceptively normal in a person with low muscle mass. Use an appropriate renal estimate for the medication and interpret it with body size, trajectory, hydration, and clinical context. Acute illness can rapidly change clearance.

Renally cleared sedatives, opioids, antibiotics, gabapentinoids, glucose-lowering agents, and anticoagulants may accumulate or require adjustment. After AKI, dehydration, or a hospitalization, reconcile doses rather than automatically resuming the old list.

Part 24 — Multimorbidity Creates Competing Recommendations

Disease-specific guidelines can produce an impossible regimen when stacked together. One therapy may improve one condition while worsening orthostasis, kidney function, continence, cognition, or treatment burden. Prioritize immediate threats, symptomatic benefit, prevention with realistic time-to-benefit, and the patient’s goals.

Ask which condition most threatens function or survival now, which treatments deliver the greatest net benefit, which recommendations conflict, and what the patient is willing and able to do. Document the reasoning when an individualized plan differs from a single-disease target.

Part 25 — What Matters Most

Do not assume every patient prioritizes longevity above independence, comfort, cognition, or remaining at home. Ask: “What health outcome is most important to you?” and “What are you unwilling to give up for more treatment?” Translate the answer into decisions.

A goal such as attending a family event, walking to the garden, avoiding hospitalization, controlling dyspnea, or staying mentally clear can guide medication intensity, rehabilitation, procedures, and follow-up. Revisit goals after major diagnoses, hospitalization, functional decline, or a change in caregiving situation.

Part 26 — Nutrition, Weight Loss, and Sarcopenia

Unintentional weight loss demands evaluation. Confirm the trajectory and assess appetite, oral health, swallowing, food access, mood, cognition, medication effects, GI symptoms, malignancy warning signs, endocrine disease, chronic infection, and ability to shop or prepare food.

Sarcopenia and malnutrition worsen weakness, falls, immunity, wound healing, and recovery. Dysphagia with coughing, wet voice, choking, recurrent pneumonia, or weight loss requires swallowing-safety evaluation. Avoid treating poor intake with a supplement while missing obstruction, depression, medication toxicity, or food insecurity.

Part 27 — Continence and Retention

Urinary incontinence can be transient or chronic and may reflect infection, delirium, diuresis, restricted mobility, constipation, medications, stress, urgency, overflow, or functional barriers. Ask about onset, pattern, dysuria, hematuria, retention symptoms, stool function, neurologic findings, and impact on goals.

Acute retention with pain, renal dysfunction, infection, or neurologic red flags needs urgent care. Avoid reflexive anticholinergic prescribing in a patient with constipation, cognitive impairment, falls, or retention risk without considering safer strategies and monitoring.

Part 28 — Sensory Loss Can Mimic Cognitive Decline

Hearing and vision impairment can produce withdrawal, misunderstanding, falls, medication errors, and poor cognitive-screen performance. Ensure glasses, hearing devices, lighting, communication access, and a quiet environment before drawing conclusions.

Sudden monocular vision loss, painful red eye with visual change, sudden hearing loss, or new neurologic deficits require urgent evaluation. Chronic sensory impairment deserves rehabilitation and environmental adaptation because it directly affects independence and safety.

Part 29 — Sleep, Pain, and Mood

Sleep disruption, poorly controlled pain, anxiety, depression, and social isolation can worsen cognition and function. Yet sedative treatment can worsen falls, respiratory suppression, and delirium. Define the syndrome, review substances and medications, address sleep disorders and pain mechanisms, and prioritize nonpharmacologic strategies when appropriate.

Ask directly about hopelessness and suicide. Older adults may present with somatic complaints, withdrawal, self-neglect, or medication nonadherence rather than naming depression. Firearm and medication access belong in a safety assessment when risk is present.

Part 30 — Elder Mistreatment

Mistreatment includes physical, sexual, psychological, and financial abuse, neglect, abandonment, and exploitation. Warning signs include unexplained injury, poor hygiene, dehydration, medication withholding, fearful interaction, controlling caregivers, inconsistent stories, missing funds, and delay in care.

Interview the patient privately when possible, assess immediate danger and capacity, document objective findings, and follow state reporting law and local adult-protective pathways. Avoid promising secrecy or confronting a suspected perpetrator in a way that increases danger. A dependent patient may need emergency protection even before every fact is known.

Part 31 — Caregiver Capacity and Strain

Caregivers may manage medications, transportation, meals, toileting, behaviors, finances, and appointments while coping with their own illness or employment. Ask what tasks they perform, what is becoming difficult, and whether backup exists. Caregiver exhaustion can create risk even without malicious intent.

Respite, home health, social work, transportation, adult day services, dementia resources, and benefits counseling can be essential treatment. Obtain the patient’s permission to include caregivers when capacity allows and protect the patient from coercion.

Part 32 — Driving and Community Mobility

Driving safety depends on vision, cognition, reaction time, strength, range of motion, medications, episodes of loss of consciousness, and actual driving behavior. Ask about crashes, near-misses, getting lost, family concern, traffic citations, and self-restriction.

Know state reporting requirements and resources for formal driving evaluation. Stopping driving without a mobility plan can increase isolation and missed care. Build alternatives such as family support, paratransit, ride programs, or delivery services while prioritizing public safety.

Part 33 — Osteoporosis and Fracture Prevention

A fragility fracture is a sentinel event and warrants evaluation beyond pain control. Assess bone health, fall mechanism, secondary causes, renal function, medications, nutrition, and future fracture risk. USPSTF recommends osteoporosis screening for women 65 or older and for younger postmenopausal women at increased risk; evidence remains insufficient for population screening in men, so use clinical judgment.

Fall prevention and bone protection are related but not identical. Exercise, home safety, vision, medication review, adequate nutrition, and appropriate osteoporosis therapy address different parts of fracture risk.

Part 34 — Prevention Must Fit Health Status

Use current screening and immunization guidance, but individualize preventive care by prior history, life expectancy, time-to-benefit, competing risks, treatment burden, and preferences. Stopping low-benefit screening is not abandonment when it is a shared, evidence-informed decision.

Vaccination remains important, but schedules and products change. Verify current CDC guidance and medical indications rather than relying on an old age cutoff. Prevention also includes exercise, oral health, hearing, vision, nutrition, mood, fall risk, and social connection.

Part 35 — Care Transitions Are High-Risk

After emergency or hospital care, compare the prehospital list, inpatient changes, discharge list, pharmacy fill history, and what the patient actually takes. Clarify stopped drugs, temporary drugs, dose changes, pending tests, follow-up appointments, equipment, wound care, diet, activity, and warning signs.

Transitions fail when nobody owns a pending culture, pathology report, repeat laboratory test, or referral. Contact the patient early, assess function and caregiver capacity, and verify that the plan is feasible. A technically correct discharge is unsafe if the patient cannot obtain medication or transfer out of bed.

Part 36 — Advance Care Planning and Serious Illness

Advance care planning explores values, surrogate decision-makers, and preferences before crisis. It is broader than code status. Confirm whether an advance directive or portable medical order exists, where it is stored, and whether the designated surrogate understands the patient’s priorities.

Palliative care can accompany disease-directed treatment at any stage of serious illness. Hospice eligibility and rules are distinct. Discuss prognosis honestly, address symptoms, and align interventions with goals without presenting comfort and treatment as mutually exclusive.

Part 37 — Board-Style Case 1: Quiet Confusion

An 82-year-old with mild dementia becomes sleepy, inattentive, and intermittently disoriented over two days after starting an over-the-counter sleep aid. The best first interpretation is hypoactive delirium with possible medication contribution—not inevitable dementia progression.

Reasoning chain: acute fluctuation + inattention + sedating or anticholinergic exposure → stabilize and search for causes → stop avoidable contributors safely → reassess cognition against baseline.

Part 38 — Board-Style Case 2: The “Mechanical” Fall

A 79-year-old taking an anticoagulant falls in the bathroom and cannot remember whether consciousness was lost. There is a scalp bruise and new headache. Calling this a simple trip is unsafe.

Reasoning chain: possible syncope + head impact + anticoagulation + symptoms → urgent evaluation for intracranial injury and the cause of the event.

Part 39 — Board-Style Case 3: Too Many Targets

An 86-year-old with frailty, recurrent falls, CKD, diabetes, hypertension, and symptomatic orthostasis takes 14 medications. The best next step is not to intensify every disease target. Clarify what matters most, reconcile the actual regimen, identify high-harm or low-benefit therapy, and build a monitored deprescribing and disease-prioritization plan.

Reasoning chain: multimorbidity + treatment burden + competing harms → prioritize safety, function, symptoms, realistic benefit, and patient goals.

Part 40 — Board-Style Case 4: “Normal” Creatinine

A thin 88-year-old becomes confused and excessively sleepy after a renally cleared medication is increased. Serum creatinine is within the laboratory reference range. Low muscle mass can mask reduced filtration, so medication accumulation remains possible.

Reasoning chain: new toxicity after dose change + low muscle mass + renal clearance → reassess kidney estimate, dose, interactions, hydration, and alternate causes urgently.

Part 41 — Board-Style Case 5: Capacity and Refusal

An older adult with mild cognitive impairment refuses a recommended procedure and accurately explains the diagnosis, options, personal risks, and reasons for choosing comfort-focused care. The diagnosis alone does not prove incapacity.

Reasoning chain: assess choice, understanding, appreciation, and reasoning for this decision → support autonomy when capacity is present → document discussion and follow-up.

Part 42 — Common Board Traps

  • Trap: Confusion in an older adult is dementia.
    Correction: acute or fluctuating inattention is delirium until a cause is evaluated.
  • Trap: A fall is explained by age.
    Correction: investigate injury, medications, gait, vision, orthostasis, cardiovascular and neurologic causes, and environment.
  • Trap: Every Beers-listed drug must be stopped immediately.
    Correction: weigh indication, harm, alternatives, withdrawal, goals, and monitoring.
  • Trap: Normal creatinine guarantees normal drug clearance.
    Correction: low muscle mass can conceal impaired filtration.
  • Trap: Dementia equals incapacity.
    Correction: capacity is decision-specific and can be supported.
  • Trap: Disease-specific targets should always be intensified.
    Correction: multimorbidity requires net-benefit and goal-based prioritization.
  • Trap: A caregiver who attends every visit guarantees safety.
    Correction: assess patient preference, caregiver capacity, coercion, and mistreatment privately when needed.
  • Trap: Palliative care means stopping all treatment.
    Correction: palliative care can accompany active disease treatment and focuses on symptoms and goals.

Part 43 — Final Board-Ready Algorithm

  1. Establish baseline and tempo: cognition, function, mobility, intake, medications, living situation, and caregiver observations.
  2. Stabilize acute threats: airway, breathing, circulation, oxygenation, glucose, neurologic deficit, trauma, bleeding, infection, and toxicity.
  3. Apply the 5Ms: Mind, Mobility, Medications, Multicomplexity, and Matters Most.
  4. Search for reversible drivers: medication effects, pain, retention, constipation, dehydration, hypoxia, metabolic disease, infection, sensory loss, and social crisis.
  5. Measure function and safety: ADLs, IADLs, gait, falls, nutrition, continence, driving, home risk, and caregiver capacity.
  6. Reconcile and prioritize treatment: indications, doses, interactions, time-to-benefit, burden, and goals.
  7. Select disposition: emergency care, hospitalization, urgent specialty review, home services, rehabilitation, or monitored outpatient care.
  8. Close the loop: teach-back, medication list, pending-result owner, transition contact, referral tracking, and reassessment of function.

High-Yield Summary

  • The Geriatrics 5Ms connect cognition, mobility, medications, complexity, and patient goals.
  • Acute fluctuating inattention is delirium until medical and toxic causes are addressed.
  • Function and trajectory often reveal severity when classic symptoms are absent.
  • Falls require injury assessment and evaluation of medications, orthostasis, gait, vision, cardiovascular and neurologic causes, and environment.
  • Polypharmacy review asks whether every drug remains indicated, effective, safe, feasible, monitored, and aligned with goals.
  • Beers Criteria support individualized judgment; they are not automatic stop orders.
  • Serum creatinine can underestimate medication risk in an older adult with low muscle mass.
  • Capacity is decision-specific; dementia does not automatically eliminate it.
  • Frailty and multimorbidity require net-benefit prioritization rather than rigid stacking of disease-specific targets.
  • Safe care depends on caregiver capacity, social support, transition quality, result ownership, and what matters most.

Evidence Anchors

  • American Geriatrics Society: Geriatrics 5Ms and current Beers Criteria resources.
  • CDC STEADI: screen, assess, and intervene to reduce older-adult fall risk.
  • U.S. Preventive Services Task Force: 2024 fall-prevention interventions and 2025 osteoporosis screening recommendations.
  • National Institute on Aging: delirium, cognition, and communication with older adults.
  • CMS and Age-Friendly Health Systems: What Matters, Medication, Mentation, and Mobility.

Clinical note: This lesson is educational and does not replace individualized assessment. Apply current AGS, CDC, USPSTF, CMS, state capacity and reporting law, local emergency pathways, renal-dose resources, and specialist or interprofessional collaboration. Acute confusion, focal neurologic deficit, severe fall injury, head trauma with bleeding risk, unstable vital signs, suspected mistreatment with immediate danger, or inability to maintain safety requires urgent escalation.
